en: The Sūtra on the Four Noble Truths Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. This...
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus! They replied:
“Yes, World-Honored One.”
“Certainly,” the bhikṣu replied,
and he listened to the Buddha.
The Buddha then spoke as follows:
“Monks! The true Dharma teaching consists of these Four Noble Truths.
They are to be fully contemplated and seen, clearly understood, analyzed, and realized through insight.”

Whatever bhikṣus there may be who have passed away from this world, they have done so from this Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, and from this Right Teaching, which consists of these Four Truths.
Possessing the vision of contemplation, one attains clear understanding and gives rise to discerning insight.

From these Four Noble Truths, whatever bhikṣus may come from future generations shall do so from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One; they shall proceed from this True Dharma, which is truly the Four Noble Truths of the noble ones.
It is as previously described.

There is currently a bhikṣu present who is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One; he too, from this same true reality, has preached these Four Noble Truths, possessing contemplative vision, having attained clear understanding, and having developed insight through discernment.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣu Śāriputra: "Bhikṣu!

There are wisdom, swift wisdom, rapid wisdom, sharp wisdom, pervasive wisdom, profound and penetrating wisdom, and unwholesome wisdom; there is also the wisdom that can see without weariness, which is followed by the wisdom of jewels."
The bhikṣu Śāriputra is capable; the bhikṣu Śāriputra has attained what is to be attained. This worthy one is proficient in the four noble truths, explaining them with complete mastery.

The bhikṣu Śāriputra is a marvelous person; he explains them fully through reflection, being able to see, able to open up, able to comprehend, and able to discern. Having distinguished and clarified his vision, he now follows the Dharma of the Path to a great extent.
This bhikṣu Śāriputra is one who is most free from transgression, for he can turn back from the wrong path.
The bhikṣu Śāriputra is able to lead others along the Path, while the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana is able to bring them to the end of the Path;
the bhikṣu Śāriputra is like a mother who gives birth, and the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana is like a mother who provides nourishment.
When the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana has awakened in this way, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, he should be served, he should be honored, and one should go to him to inquire.
"Śāriputra and the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana have brought forth thoughts of loving-kindness for their fellow students, ensuring that no other [unwholesome] thoughts arise.
After the Buddha had spoken thus, he rose from his seat, entered his chamber, and remained there for a while in contemplation.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, for the sake of benefit and so that the Buddha might remain in the world, now spoke these Four Noble Truths:
"What are the four? [They are as follows:]"
The first is suffering, the second is its origin, the third is its cessation, and the fourth is the path; by practicing these Four Noble Truths, one brings suffering to an end.
What are they, worthy sir?
The Truth of Suffering:

suffering arising from birth, suffering arising from old age, suffering as illness, suffering as death; suffering from encountering what one dislikes, suffering from being separated from what one loves, and the failure to obtain what one seeks—these are also sufferings; furthermore, there are the five kinds of suffering that arise suddenly.
"Venerable sir!
What is the arising of suffering?

When a person belongs to this or that class of beings, and through the process of birth there is further increase, such that, by way of becoming, the five aggregates have arisen and the life-faculty has been obtained—this is called 'birth'."
Birth, O worthy one,
is suffering.
By what cause and condition does suffering arise?

For one who is born, because the body exists, there is contact, which leads to further contact; from contact comes further contact, and from feeling comes further feeling, causing the mind to experience further suffering.
From contact comes further contact, and from sensation comes further sensation, causing both body and mind to experience further suffering.
From contact to further contact, one knows feeling after feeling, causing the body to endure the affliction of feeling.
From contact to further contact, one perceives feeling after feeling, and the mental faculty becomes feverish and afflicted.
From contact to further contact, one knows feeling after feeling, causing the body and mind to burn with affliction.
From contact to further contact, from suffering to further suffering, the body burns with exhaustion and affliction.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, the mind becomes feverish, distressed, and exhausted with heat and sorrow.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, the body and mind become distressed, feverish, and exhausted.
From the feverish distress of perception, from contact to further contact, and from feeling to further feeling, birth arises, O worthy one!
Suffering is spoken of as suffering upon suffering; therefore it is said that from this there is aging.
“Wise one! What is this that is called aging?

That which is the exhaustion of each individual person—that is aging. It is being wrinkled and white-haired, with failing strength; it is being hunched and leaning on a staff, with hair falling out and gray spots appearing; it is the faculties having matured, the body being on the verge of collapse, the complexion having changed, and the lifespan having run its course—this is what is called aging.”
"Aging, O worthy one,
is suffering.
For what reason and by what causal condition is aging said to be suffering?"

Because the human body undergoes further suffering through repeated contact (*phassa*), and through repeated contact, feeling (*vedanā*) arises again and again; the mind also experiences further suffering.
Through repeated contact, formations (*saṅkhāra*) arise again and again, and through these formations, feeling arises again and again; thus, both body and mind experience suffering.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, the body is tormented by fever.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, the mind is tormented by fever.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, both body and mind are tormented by fever.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, there arises bodily heat, fatigue, and distress.
From mutual contact to further mutual contact, from mutual feeling to further mutual feeling, there arises mental fever, affliction, fatigue, and sorrow.
From contact to contact, from feeling to feeling, there arise bodily and mental fever, fatigue, and distress.
From contact to contact, from feeling to further feeling—for this reason, O worthy one!
He speaks of the suffering of old age.
Having previously spoken of suffering, for this reason he says:
"Sickness, worthy one!"
Suffering.
What constitutes illness?

There is illness of the head, illness of the abdomen, illness of the ears, illness of the nose, illness of the mouth, illness of the lips, illness of the tongue, illness of the throat, illness of hiccups, illness of transformation, illness of the lower parts, feverish illness, illness of urinary discharge, epilepsy, illness of goiters, recurring illness, illness of the joints, illness of the skin, illness of the fat, illness of blood-heat, and illness of phlegm; there are also many others like these, all born of attachment (*upādāna*), from which one cannot escape, and all of which reside within the body.
"Sickness, worthy one!
Is suffering.
By what causes and conditions does the suffering of sickness arise?"

Because a person experiences sensation, the body undergoes further suffering; from contact there is further contact, and from sensation there is further sensation, such that the mind and mental factors experience suffering.
From contact there is further contact, and from sensation there is further sensation, so that both body and mind experience further suffering.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, the body is tormented by heat.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, the mind is tormented by heat.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, both body and mind are tormented by heat.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, there is bodily heat, fatigue, and distress.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, there is mental heat, fatigue, and distress.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, there arises bodily and mental fever, fatigue, and distress.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, O worthy one, that which is called "sickness" arises.
It is suffering.
Therefore it is said: "It also arises from these causes and conditions.
Death, O worthy one!"
Suffering.

What is death? When a person exists, and that person who exists within the cycle of birth and death discards the body, undergoes ruin, and perishes in every place; when one no longer sees life, the five aggregates have already been exhausted, the life-faculty has already been abandoned, and at the time of death it has already ceased—this is called death.
"Venerable sir!
Regarding suffering, what is the cause and condition for the suffering of death?

When a person dies, they experience further suffering through bodily contact; from contact there is further contact, and from sensation there is further sensation, such that their mental intention experiences further suffering."
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, the body and mind experience suffering.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, they cause the body to be feverish and distressed.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, they cause the mind to be tormented by feverish distress.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, they cause both body and mind to be tormented by feverish distress.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, the body becomes feverish, weary, regretful, and afflicted.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, the body and the mental faculty become feverish, weary, regretful, and afflicted.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling.
"Death, O worthy one!
is suffering"—this is spoken because of these causes and conditions, and it is also spoken because of these causes and conditions.
“Meeting with those one does not love is suffering, O worthy one!
In what way is meeting with those one does not love so? [It is] as follows:”
"O Wise One!
There are six internal bases of human beings; it is not possible to avoid them, for from these they meet and encounter one another.
Possessing this characteristic of disintegration—separation from those with whom one was once joined, and parting from those with whom one shared common affairs—this is suffering."

In this same way, it is so for the external as well; it is so for consciousness, so for volition, so for feeling, so for perception, so for mental formations, so for craving, and so for the six modes of conduct.
There is, worthy one!
A person who, through six kinds of grasping, does not feel sorrow.
What are these six kinds?
Whether it be the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, or the consciousness element—
this coming together, this conjoining, this meeting, and this collective activity constitute suffering.
To encounter what one does not love, worthy sir,
is suffering.
For what reason, worthy sir, is encountering what one does not love suffering?
Is it suffering?
It is not being able to associate with those one does not love. Wise one!
A person causes the body to experience further suffering through repeated contact, and through repeated feeling, causes the mind to experience further suffering.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, they cause the body and mind to experience renewed suffering.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, they cause the body and mind to experience renewed feverish distress.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, they cause the body to become feverish, exhausted, and afflicted with suffering.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, they cause the mind to become feverish, exhausted, and afflicted with suffering.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, one causes the body, mind, and thoughts to become heated, exhausted, pained, and distressed.
From contact to further contact, from feeling to further feeling, there is no meeting with mutual compassion, O Worthy One!
It is suffering.
Therefore, what has been said also proceeds from this; thus it is said from this:
"The characteristic of separation is sorrowful, O worthy one!"
Suffering.
What is the sorrow of separation?
There is such a thing, worthy one!

That which is created by humans, that which one enters into with sorrow, and that from which one must undergo separation and loss—this separation of characteristics, this dissociation, not being together, not dwelling in common, not meeting, and not encountering again: this is suffering.

In this same way, it is so for the external as well; consciousness is thus, further craving is thus, sensation is thus, perception is thus, volition is thus, craving is thus, and the six bases are thus.
"There is, worthy one! A person possesses six bases:

the earth-base, the water-base, the fire-base, the wind-base, the space-base, and the consciousness-base. When one is separated from these bases, when they are distinct, dissociated, not meeting, far removed, not dwelling together, not encountering, and not mutually experienced—this is suffering."
This is detachment, O Venerable One!
Suffering is for this reason taught, and it is also taught because of these causes and conditions.
"If one seeks and does not obtain, that too is suffering"; therefore, it is further taught.
"Worldly phenomena, worthy one!
For a person, if a mental sprout has arisen, it should not be produced; this too may be abandoned.
Aging, worthy one!"
For a person, such as this, the desire for birth is a root that does not age; this intention is not abandoned.

O worthy one! For a person subject to the nature of illness, once illness has been experienced, there is the desire for birth, thinking, "May I not have it," and there is the desire to abandon suffering, thinking, "May this pain cease."
Regarding the nature of death, venerable sir, when a person is subject to death, even if they have the desire, "May I not die," they cannot escape it.
This is so, venerable sir.

When a person experiences pain that is undesirable, ungraspable, and disagreeable to the mind, they desire that what has arisen be produced; yet because that pain is undesirable, ungraspable, and disagreeable to the mind, they seek to make it desirable, to make it graspable, and to make it agreeable to the mind, failing to achieve this. From such desire, [suffering] is cut off.

"There is, worthy one! When a person seeks out thoughts, they also reflect that it is improper and not to be intended; such a thought should not arise. To cause such a thought to arise, one seeks out thoughts that are improper and unintended, desiring that this thought be so; yet because it is intended and deemed proper, one cannot prevent this thought from being used and deemed proper, and thus one does not attain its cessation. From this, one attains its abandonment."
"There is such a thing, worthy one!

There is contact that is agreeable and pleasing; if such a state of mind arises, and this contact already arisen is agreeable and pleasing, one would wish it to remain forever and never depart, and one would not desire its cessation."
Furthermore, worthy one!

Suppose a person gives rise to this thought, conceiving a desire for what is agreeable and desirable; having given rise to this thought, they conceive a desire for what is agreeable and desirable, and they ensure that this thought remains constant, firm, and inseparable, and that this aspiration is never severed.
Not obtaining what one seeks is also suffering; therefore it is said, and for this reason it is taught from these causes and conditions.
"The five aggregates are originally suffering"; therefore it is further taught so that one may follow this Dharma.

These phenomena are impermanent; they are destroyed by calamity and disease, and are characterized by sickness, decay, old age, lack of solidity, unreliability, desire, transformation, and separation. For this reason, the five aggregates are fundamentally suffering.
In the past, worthy one, this was the noble truth of suffering; in the future, worthy one, this will be the noble truth of suffering;
and in the present, worthy one, this is the noble truth of suffering.
This is also the Truth of Suffering; it is without difference, non-erroneous, and non-delusive.
As it is the truth and as it is suchness, so this suchness is the noble truth, the noble truth.
"Venerable one!
This is the truth known through vision and attained through realization; such is the awakening to the truth. Therefore, it is called the 'Truth of the Venerable One.
What, venerable one, is this?"
"Is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
There is, venerable sir!
When one is fond of the six internal bases of contact and dwells attached to them, this is the origin."
As with one's own body, so it is with external bodies; consciousness further knows and perceives them with compassion.
Furthermore, worthy one, a person possesses craving for the six bases:
First is earth, second is water, third is fire, fourth is wind, fifth is space, and sixth is consciousness.
That which one loves and clings to arises through association and proximity; this is called "habitual accumulation" (*saṃskāra*).
What should one do in such a case?

If a person has sons, as well as a wife, servants, drivers, fields, houses, shops, and bedding, yet he ceases to find delight in them, and instead becomes attached to what is near and goes forth to seek more—know that this craving is the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

In the past, O worthy one, that time was also a conditioning of craving, a conditioning of suffering, and a conditioning of the worthy one; in the future, O worthy one, that time will also be a conditioning of craving, a conditioning of suffering, and a conditioning of the worthy one; and in the present, O worthy one, this time is also a conditioning of craving, a conditioning of suffering, and a conditioning of the worthy one.
Thus it is not otherwise; as it is, so it is not inverted or delusive, but is the true reality just as it is.
There is, O worthy one!
Truth; for the worthy one, this truth is to be seen, understood, attained, realized, and fully awakened to.
Therefore, the noble truth of the origin of suffering is called the truth of the noble ones. "And what, noble one,
is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?"
"There is, worthy one!

For a person, there are six bases of contact within oneself that are not grasped; by being liberated from them, not experiencing them further, having already severed them, abandoned them, become detached from them, exhausted them, no longer looking toward them, extinguished them, and brought them to stillness, this is the cessation of suffering."
Thus it is with the internal body, and so too with the external; consciousness approaches, further conceptualizes, forms intentions, and harbors expectations, and craving is likewise.
There is, O worthy one!
A person possesses six elements that are not to be craved:
first, earth; second, water; third, fire; fourth, wind; fifth, space; and sixth, consciousness.

Through these one attains liberation—no longer experiencing them, having already severed, abandoned, discarded, transformed, and rendered useless them—this is the stillness that constitutes the end of suffering.

What, then, is this? If a person is without craving and attachment—whether toward children, the household, servants, drivers, fields, houses, dwellings, shops, bedding, or the profits from buying and selling—and is without such attachment, does not associate with them, and does not give rise to the desire for them; when there is no more of this, one should know that this is the Noble Truth that the exhaustion of craving is the exhaustion of suffering.
In the past, O worthy one!

at that time, this too was the noble truth that the exhaustion of craving is the exhaustion of suffering; it is likewise in the future, and in the present time as well, this is the noble truth that the exhaustion of craving is the exhaustion of suffering.
Thus it is not otherwise; as it is, so it is without delusion and without inversion. This suchness is the reality; therefore, the complete exhaustion of suffering is called the Noble Truth.
"What, O Noble One, is this?"
“Is there, venerable sir, a Noble Truth of the practice leading to the end of suffering? “There is, venerable sir;
it is the Eightfold Path.”
1. Right view, 2. right resolve, 3. right speech, 4. right action, 5. right livelihood, 6. right effort, 7. right mindfulness, and 8. right concentration.
"What, worthy one, is right view?
If, worthy one..."

The virtuous disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path. He attains analytical observation, is able to attain the observation of phenomena (*dharma*), is able to receive and contemplate mental formations (*saṃjñā*), is able to be mindful of them, and is able to practice accordingly; this is called right view.

Furthermore, one contemplates the observance of precepts, recollects the Way and its Virtue, and swiftly practices the path of seeing. One repents of what has been received and brings it to rest; one dwells in non-action, mindfulness, and tranquility. One ceases following attachment, as if having attained liberation. With the mind discerning and contemplating the characteristics of practice, the mind remains focused on the Dharma. Contemplating characteristics without being separated from them, one experiences their convergence; this is called upright view, and this is called the Truth of the Way and its Virtue.
"What, venerable sir,
is upright governance?
If, venerable sir..."

A moral disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; if they practice by following these reflections with repeated mindfulness, this is called "straightforward cultivation."

Furthermore, one contemplates past lives, maintains what has been learned, recollects the characteristics of practice, contemplates remorse through conduct, attains the unconditioned and tranquility, achieves cessation through non-attachment, gains liberation of mind, and contemplates cessation; whatever is sought, whatever is dedicated, and whatever thoughts and practices follow—this is called "straightforward governance," and this is called the "Truth of the Path."
"What, worthy one, is upright speech?
It is the same, worthy one."
Virtuous disciple!

Whether contemplating suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation, or the path as the path, you should cease the four verbal transgressions and other remaining evil verbal actions; from this, you shall attain cessation and detachment.
Cessation, detachment, restraint, and non-action—by not acting, one incurs no offense from what has been undertaken; there being no offense, having already ceased, this is called right speech.

Furthermore, one maintains the contemplation of what was previously observed; having entered into the practice of walking in mindfulness of the Path, one turns away from the intention of regret regarding those practices toward the unconditioned, the transcendence of the world, tranquility, contentment, cessation, and non-attachment. Just as one who has attained liberation contemplates with discernment, one eliminates the four types of verbal misconduct, distancing oneself from them, ceasing them, becoming detached from them, guarding against them, refraining from what should not be done, and no longer committing acts that lead to the reception of retribution. Being free from guilt and having brought such actions to rest—this is called right speech; this is called the Truth of the Path and its Fruit.
"What, venerable sir, is right conduct?
It is mindfulness, venerable sir."

A virtuous disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path. He abandons the three unwholesome bodily actions and all other unwholesome bodily actions; by ceasing them, departing from them, restraining them, and not performing them—thereby ending what would have been sinful and remaining free from sin—he has brought them to rest. This is called "straight conduct."

Furthermore, one maintains the contemplation of past lives and acts in accordance with the path of virtue. Recalling the conduct of the world, one perceives its regrettable nature; one abides in cessation, in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and in the vision of transcending the world. One attains tranquil stillness, transcends the world through the unconditioned, and remains unattached. Having attained liberation as intended, one contemplates and eliminates the three types of bodily misconduct, as well as all evil bodily actions. Through detachment, cessation, separation, restraint, and the realization that such acts should not be performed, one is freed from the accumulation of offenses. When offenses have ceased, this is called "right conduct" (*samyak-pratipad*), and this is called the "truth of the path of virtue" (*mārga-satya*).
“What, venerable sir,
is upright action?
If, venerable sir,”

A virtuous disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, the origin of suffering as its origin, the cessation of suffering as its cessation, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as the practice of the path. That which should not be sought and that which should not be practiced—namely, various animal-like actions performed through wrong conduct for the sake of sustaining one's life—is called wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*).

Furthermore, one maintains the contemplation of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa-anusmṛti*) and attains the Way through such practice. One reflects upon worldly conduct with remorse, practicing cessation, transcendence of the world, and the contemplation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Being tranquil, one attains cessation and transcends the world; being unattached, as if having attained liberation, one follows this contemplation. One should neither seek nor not seek. Regarding the various karmic actions of animals by which they sustain their lives, one should abandon them, cease from them, distance oneself from them, restrain oneself, and refrain from performing them. From receiving retribution, there shall be nothing more; once the offense has ceased, this is called upright action (*ṛju-karman*), and this is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
“What, worthy one, is upright skillful means? Worthy one,
[it is as follows:]”

A virtuous disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path. Whatever diligence, skillful means, exertion, steadfastness, capability, application, and joy he possesses—his mindfulness being neither corrupted nor extinguished, remaining in right stillness—this is called "straightforward skillful means."

Furthermore, there is the contemplation of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa-anusmṛti*), as well as the attainment of mindfulness in practice; from the worldly course of action, one perceives remorse, ceases [worldly views], transcends the world, becomes unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), tranquil, follows cessation, is non-attached, and has attained the contemplation of liberation through the path. Whatever diligence, skillful means (*upāya*), emergence, abiding, spreading, joy, and the non-destruction of mindfulness there is—properly gathered and stilled—this is called upright skillful means; this is called the truth of the Way and its Virtue (*mārga-guṇa-satya*).
"What, venerable sir,
is right mindfulness?
If, venerable sir..."

A virtuous disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; they contemplate these characteristics with mindfulness, maintaining constant recollection without forgetting. Speaking little and never departing from mindfulness—this is called upright mindfulness.

Furthermore, one contemplates the retention of past lives and proceeds from the practice of attaining the Way. One reflects that worldly actions are not to be regretted, and maintains concentration, cessation, transcendence of the world, unconditionedness, tranquility, the stopping of views, singular virtue, non-attachment, and a mind like liberation. Through the contemplation of mental objects, one follows every thought, remains mindful without forgetfulness, speaks little, and does not depart from mindfulness. This is called "straight and correct mindfulness," and this is called the "Truth of the Path and Virtue."
"What, venerable sir,
is right concentration?
If, venerable sir..."

The virtuous disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, the origin as the origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path. Because the foundations of mindfulness are established, he is neither shaken nor distracted; having attained composure through restraint, his mind and thoughts are focused on a single point—this is called right concentration.

Furthermore, one contemplates the retention of past lives and attains liberation through the faculty of mindfulness. Seeing the conduct of the world, one feels remorse; one gathers, ceases, transcends the world, becomes unconditioned, sees things as they truly are, and attains non-attachment. Following the causes and conditions of liberation, one directs the mind toward the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Being rightly settled, undeluded, not wandering, gathered, and ceased, with mindfulness and concentration fixed upon the two thoughts—this is called "right concentration" (*samyaksamādhi*), and this is called the "Truth of the Path."

In past lives, O worthy one, this was the Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering that you accepted; in future lives, O worthy one, it shall likewise be the Noble Truth of suffering that you accept and practice; and in the present life, O worthy one, it is likewise the Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering that you accept and practice. Thus it is not otherwise, not different, not lost, and not confused; it is the true reality as it has been from the beginning, the reality of the Dharma as it possesses virtue. O worthy one!
When one perceives these truths again and attains liberation accordingly, this is therefore called the exhaustion of suffering (*duḥkhakṣaya*).
The practice proceeding from this is termed the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
To summarize from the subsequent perspective, there is the perception of suffering, the origin of suffering, its cessation, and likewise the path; the practices taught by the Buddha are immeasurable.
When Śāriputra had spoken thus, the bhikṣus received and practiced it.

Regarding the contemplation of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), the *Mahānānapaṭipada Sūtra* states: "To believe in the fundamental causes and conditions, knowing that [the present] arises from past lives, is called 'right view' (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)."
The *Yijue* states: "Knowing past events" is like the case of future events.
This is as taught by the Buddha in the *Catuḥsatya-sūtra*.
